prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing neutral-atom frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B003 to B024. My first-round case for B003 was a real scientific one, a specific prediction followed by an unexpected discovery, and I still hold it. What changed is the weighing of maturity and exact credit after reading the whole exchange. The lattice clock rests on one concrete idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trap, and on a realization that has been independently reproduced at the 1e-18 level in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) with different atoms. This is the robustness I ask of any result in my own field: a number that other groups reproduce and that does not depend on a model. Every file that discusses the ballot names the same two people, which is rare on this list. Five colleagues who know the field better than I do prefer it, and the points they raise against it (overlap with 2005 and 2012, pending redefinition) are the same points I raised myself in round 1, so I am not hearing a new objection that should keep me where I was. A citation that names the lattice scheme and its realization at 1e-18 does not need the redefinition of the second and does not need to claim a new state of matter.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is the one I made in round 1: a lattice clock is a quantitative leap in a capability that earlier prizes (the 2005 comb, the 2012 ion control) already opened, and it is not a new physical regime. I would still weigh a new phase of matter above a precision step in the abstract. Credit also has loose ends. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley each made early demonstrations, and a two-name credit will be read as a choice. I am not an atomic physicist and have not checked the first-demonstration dates myself. Against B003 as my lead: the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, Yuan Cao and other early experimenters fall outside any three-name credit, and several colleagues who know the field better than I do want a few more years of consolidation. I do not think those reasons should block B003 forever, but they make it the better second-year or later candidate than the better 2026 candidate.

responses.point: Eva presents the clock as one clear idea with independent reproduction at 1e-18, argues the many-body and interaction studies inside the clock show it asks new questions about nature, and flags her own closeness to the field and the open priority question for Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley.
responses.response: Your answer to my round-1 worry about novelty is what moved me. If the clock is valued because it lets us study interactions and many-body effects in a controlled lattice and resolve redshifts across millimetres, then it is not only a refinement. I also accept that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover the neutral-atom lattice idea. On credit I would ask you, as the person closest to the literature, to say whether Lemonde and the NIST group contributed independent ideas or independent demonstrations. If it is demonstrations of Katori's scheme, I am comfortable that the invention sits with Katori and the record-accuracy work with Ye. I would phrase the citation on the scheme and the 1e-18 realization, and I would not add many-body physics to the credited achievement unless you and Stefan think it is essential, because that would invite a harder dispute about who did what.

responses.point: Stefan states that Ye's role in the record accuracy is partly engineering and systematic control building on Katori's concept, and that the committee must decide whether to credit that as invention, while also saying the redefinition of the second should not be a condition.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether the redefinition is a necessary condition. Your answer, backed by Eva and Mark, is that it is not, and I accept that: the criterion should be demonstrated, independently confirmed performance. On your point about Ye, I do not think systematic control at 1e-18 is routine engineering. It is the part that tells us the number is real, and in my own field the equivalent is the work that shows different codes agree. That is science, and it is why I am comfortable with Ye as the second name. I would, however, keep the citation wording on realization and accuracy, not on a vague word like 'invention' alone, so that the two contributions are visible. Your note about Boulder and Hall's lineage is worth the committee's attention, but I read it as a weak connection and not a reason for you to step back.

responses.point: Ulf ranks B003 slightly higher because it opened a field of new physics, while accepting that B024 is cleanest on attribution and maturity and that he would be content to see it first.
responses.response: We made the same argument in round 1 and I do not retract it: a prediction answered by nature is the pattern I find most convincing. But you wrote that you would be content with B024 first, and I now think that is where the weight of the exchange lies. The mechanism question is not a bar in principle, and I still would not impose it, but the credit question for Cao is a real one and Eva, Stefan and Eva Olsson want more consolidation. Waiting a few years costs B003 little, since the field is not going away. I would like us both to say plainly that this is a matter of sequence and not a verdict against B003, and I would keep B003 as my first alternative. A two-part B003 plus B024 prize cannot be written within three names, so I do not propose it.

responses.point: Mark notes that broad support is not the same as merit, that three members ranked B024 sixth or seventh, and that the credit will be read as a choice among a wider clock community, and asks that the case not lean on the redefinition.
responses.response: I was one of the three who ranked it low at opening, so I take your point about support counts, and I do not move because five colleagues prefer it. I move because the reasons they give are scientific: an idea, a measurement tied to independent confirmation, and a short, shared attribution. I agree that the citation should not rely on the redefinition of the second or on the geodesy applications, since they are expected uses and not yet the achievement. I would accept the wording 'invention and realization of optical lattice clocks' and the 1e-18 level as the measure of what was demonstrated. The two-name credit will be a choice, as you say, but I think it is a defensible one, with the early demonstrations of Lemonde and others acknowledged in the committee's background text and not in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Hinkley hold a claim to the first demonstrations strong enough to disturb a two-name credit; I defer to the atomic physicists and have not verified priority dates.
Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as a continuation; I give this real weight.

Whether B003 should have been preferred this year if the superconducting mechanism is clarified soon; I would revisit it if the mechanism becomes better established or the credit question for Cao is answered.
How the committee should treat Yuan Cao and other early experimental groups under a three-person limit if B003 is considered in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is a known collaborator, student or colleague of mine. I work in electronic-structure theory, not atomic or precision physics, and have not recused myself on any ballot.
